maintopic: CANADIAN N ATIONAL-C AN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 13, consideration of the motion of Hon. R. J. Manion for the second reading of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific railway system, and for other purposes.

maintopic: CANADIAN N ATIONAL-C AN ADI AN PACIFIC RAILWAY BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue the debate on the motion for the second reading of the measure now before the house let me say that I do not intend to deal very extensively with the bill as it now appears. While I intend to express my opinion later on with regard to certain phases of the measure I wish to confine myself now to certain omissions on the part of the Duff commission and to a certain lack of consideration on the part of those responsible for the preparation of this bill. Before doing so, however, in common with other hon. members who have spoken so eloquently I wish to compliment the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) on the very fair manner in which he presented this bill to the house. His speech was on a very high plane; he appealed to the house to lay aside partisanship, saying that the situation was so serious that every hon. member in this house should give this bill his very best consideration. The hon. gentleman zealously avoided anything that savoured of politics or partisanship, and his appeal was immediately answered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) whose remarks also were on a high level. The right hon. gentleman offered certain criticisms, but he expressed the hope that they would be received in good part, with the knowledge that he was endeavouring to better the measure and make it more operative.
I am glad to be able to pay this compliment to the Minister of Railways and Canals, but I very much regret that I cannot say the same thing with regard to his leader, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett), who undertook to give this house a history of railway construction in this country. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister refer to the terms under which the Intercolonial railway was built, because later on In my remarks I desire to direct the attention of the house to this question. The Prime Minister brought his history of railway construction down to 1914, and directed especial attention to the construction of the railways through western Canada, but when the right hon. gentleman came to 1914 he stopped like grandfather's clock, never to go again. He contented himself with the introduction of the political element into the discussion at that point. The right hon. gentleman said that the Liberal government had subsidized the construction of the Canadian Northern from a point in Ontario to Winnipeg and that, he said, was the beginning of our troubles. Is it possible that the hectic times through which the Prime Minister and his government are passing have shortened his memory? Why did he not give the full history of railroad construction in this country instead of stopping at 1914? Has my right hon. friend forgotten those days we witnessed in parliament in 1914 when he, as a supporter of the Conservative government of that day, derided and berated an hon. gentleman now sitting in another chamber because he introduced a measure that had for its object the construction of the Canadian Northern from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast? Has the Prime Minister forgotten that during that debate he used every condemnatory adjective in the English language? Has he forgotten that he pointed out that the measure meant the creation of a corruption fund; that it would bring about the corruption of the electorate of the Dominion of Canada? Has he forgotten what he called the disgraceful lobbying carried on by Mackenzie and Mann in the corridors of this parliament in order to corrupt the members of the House of Commons? But that measure went through, Mr. Speaker, and that was the beginning of all our troubles; it provided for the establish-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Veniot
ment of the third transcontinental railway in Canada, and from that day to this we have had troubles galore.
The Prime Minister must have had an object in view. I do not wish to impute motives, Mr. Speaker, because that is against the rules of the house, but one cannot help but suspect that the reason the Prime Minister did not give the full history of railway construction in Canada was that if he did so he would not be able to lay the blame on the Liberal party for the transportation problem facing this country to-day. The introduction of that element of politics into the discussion by the Prime Minister has thrown a shadow over this house. The right hon. gentleman should have known that we of the opposition would not allow him to throw into our faces any blame which did not belong to us. As a result of his speech we on this side of the house have been driven to recrimination; we have been forced to define our position, and as a result the debate has not remained on the high level on which it began. I hope that as the debate continues we will get back to the point of view we had in the beginning. Of all men in this country the Prime Minister should have set the example; he should have taken a leaf from the book of his Minister of Railways, but perhaps the Minister of Railways did not consult the Prime Minister and did not make known to him the position he would assume during this debate. But knowing the Prime Minister as we do on this side of the house; knowing that he always glories when he is in a position to attack, knowing that he always feels justified in using recrimination, sarcasm and invective when he is dealing with the arguments of his political opponents, we are not at all surprised that he reached such a level in the debate.
Now, having treated that part of the Prime Minister's speech, I shall refer as briefly as possible to what I consider an omission on the part of the Duff commission in dealing with the railway situation in Canada so far as it relates to the human element. And when I say human element, I am not thinking of the men who were discharged in the past, or of those who are going to be laid off in the future in the interest of economy. We are to-day faced with a situation so serious in connection with our railways that economies have become absolutely necessary. Some sacrifices will have to be made. No doubt our railway employees will find it hard when they are retired and have no longer any work on the railways but must seek employment elsewhere, perhaps at work to which they have not been accustomed. But be that

as it may, be the sacrifice as great as it may, sacrifices all round have to be made and no doubt in the long run these men will understand that they too, forming an integral part of the dominion, will have to bear their fair share of the burden.
But there is another point of view from the human side of the case, and I wish now to refer to what is known as the provident or insurance fund. I speak now with reference to the Canadian National railway system. I see nothing in either this bill or the report of the commission that would in any way protect the men who have been laid off in the past or those who will necessarily be laid off in the future. Under the system now in vogue the railway employee contributing to the provident fund must put in fifteen years of service continuously, and any time he loses in that period is deducted from his fifteen years. He must serve fifteen years before he can claim any of the privileges under the fund, unless through sickness or accident, and on the proper certificate of a doctor. Men who have been fourteen years in the service are being laid off, and dismissal is1 in accordance with the principle of seniority; the lesser the number of years a man has in the service the sooner he is liable to be laid off under the regulations adopted by the railways and by the labour unions associated with them. If under this system a man has not completed his fifteen years and is laid off through no fault of his own, it is absolutely impossible for him to draw any benefit from the provident fund or insurance. The amount he has contributed remains in the fund for the benefit of those who are fortunate enough to be kept permanently employed.
Now I want to put this proposition to the Minister of Railways and to every member of this house. Is it fair or just that men who are retired before the time at which they can claim compensation, provided they are qualified for proper retirement under the Pension Act, should be laid aside and have nothing provided for them in the way of compensation out of the very fund to which they have been contributing for perhaps fourteen years? I want the minister to look carefully into this matter, because there is uneasiness to-day among the railway em-. ployees throughout the country. They fear that because this bill does not deal with that situation, because the Duff commission which investigated the railway problem has not seen fit to consider the question or to make any recommendations in regard to it, those who may be retired before the completion of their
29S5

CN.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Veniot
fifteen years will lose what they have contributed. True, under the system, ordinarily speaking, if they retired before the end of the fifteen years they would not be entitled; but that would be voluntary on their part. To-day, however, they are being laid off through no fault of their own, as a result of that regime of economy which the government feels called upon to establish in the administration of the railways. Surely these men should not be allowed to suffer to such an extent that they are unable to benefit from the amounts which they themselves have contributed to the fund.
There is another point with regard to the human element, and that is the question of seniority. I would call the attention of the minister to this point, No mention is made of the situation which will result from the recommendations of the Duff report with regard to the seniority of these men. Ordinarily under the rules, a man who is laid off for a period of more than one year-I think it is one year, but it may be eighteen months;
I am subject to correction in this regard-loses his seniority. In this case if he is laid off he may not be called again to resume work on the railways for two or three years, until such time as conditions improve and they require more men; and the very moment a man is called upon to resume work he loses all seniority and has to begin at the bottom of the ladder and work his way up again. That is not fair.

-before the bill passes out of the committee stage and comes up for third reading. I should like to have him call in the railway men, representatives from the different railway unions who are familiar with the operations of the fund and with the question of seniority, so as to satisfy himself that I am either right or wrong. If I am wrong, then I shall feel that at least I have done my duty in bringing the matter to the attention of the government, so that the responsible minister will be able when the time comes to assure parliament and the people of Canada that no injustice will be done these men.
I come now to a consideration of the Intercolonial railway, to which both the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition referred in their speeches. I am not going to tire the house with a detailed history of that enterprise. The Intercolonial railway became the bond between the maritime provinces and old Canada, known at that time as Quebec and Ontario. In 1864 New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island met in conference at Charlottetown to decide whether they should link up as a union of the maritime provinces with one government or remain as three separate colonies. When Quebec and Ontario heard of this conference they sent delegates to Charlottetown to appeal to the maritime provinces not to consummate the union. They pointed out that Ontario and Quebec must obtain transportation for their products through Canadian ports to the markets across the sea. They pointed out that the manufacturers of Ontario were at the mercy of the American railways. This did not seem to convince the maritime provinces, but Quebec and Ontario went still further. They appealed to their patriotism and to their loyalty to the British crown. They pledged themselves that if the maritime provinces would forego union they on their part would agree that the Intercolonial railway would be built from a point on the St. Lawrence to the port of Halifax, with a connecting branch line to the port of Saint John. This railway was to be built not only for the accommodation of the people in Quebec and Ontario but it was promised that the commerce going through the ports of the maritimes would bring prosperity to those provinces such as they had never had before.
At that time the maritime provinces were enjoying the height of prosperity. The American markets along the New England coast were open to them and they were the most prosperous section of British North America. However, we were willing to forego that prosperity in order to uphold the greater supremacy of the British Empire. From that day to this although at times there has been uneasiness exhibited in the maritime provinces, nowhere under the British flag will you find people more loyal to the British crown than the people of the three provinces down by the sea. No matter what our differences may have been, no matter how much uneasiness has been created in past years in the maritime provinces because of a lack of fulfilment of the promises of confederation, no matter how much unwarranted ill treatment there has been of the maritime provinces by the central provinces of Canada, there are to be found in the maritime provinces people without

number who are prepared to stand by confederation. and do everything they can to bring about betterment in the conditions of this country.
We have sacrificed much in the maritime provinces and about ten years ago this burden became so heavy that an agitation was commenced for better terms. That agitation resulted in the appointment of the Duncan commission, and the report of that commission was laid before parliament in 1927 or 1928. The recommendations of this report were implemented to such an extent that the uneasiness gradually began to disappear, and I think I am right in saying that to-day that uneasiness has almost totally disappeared.
If under the terms of the measure now before the house the identity of the Intercolonial railway is to be lost and the government is to have no control over it, then I say the government is doing violence to the act of confederation and to the agreement arrived at at the London conference in December, 1866. It was because of the terms arrived at at that conference that the maritime provinces consented to come into confederation. I refer those who do not know the history of the maritime provinces to section 145 of the British North America Act. What will they find there? I shall not take time to read it all, but in substance this section lays down the reasons why Nova Scotia and New Brunswick came into confederation. The promise of the construction of the Intercolonial railway to link up old Canada with the maritime provinces is definitely set out in section 145 as one of the terms under which we came into confederation.
From that date down to 1912 there was no attempt made to run the old Intercolonial as a paying institution. Even though the freight rates were low there were years of surpluses in that period. Out of twenty-five years of service there were some sixteen years of surpluses and eight or nine years of very small deficits. Those who have used the argument in the. past that the Intercolonial was the sink hole of our railway system did not know what they were talking about.
Let me go one step further in this respect. This bill gives absolute power to the board of trustees to lease any section of the Canadian National road. Up to the present time the government of Canada have never lost their hold upon the Intercolonial. I know it will be said that under the present system they have, but I contend that they have not. The Canadian National system was established in 1919 and the Intercolonial was not included in the bill which amended the 1919 act and extended the area of operation of the (Mr. Veniot.]
Canadian National Railways. Why? Because it was considered as a distinct bond of confederation and so stated in the British North America Act and in the agreement arrived at at the London conference. The London conference took place in December of 1866 and from that date until 1928-those who took part in the conference were all dead in 1928 -only a very few knew just what were the deliberations of that conference. It was a complete secret, kept from the maritime provinces. Why? Because the London conference was not in all respects in accord with the conference held in the city of Quebec in 1865. It was only in 1928 that a supposed copy of the original was discovered in an attic in a parliament building in the maritime provinces. It was forwarded to London for verification and when the verification came back, the government of Canada in 1928 had a print made and placed in this book in the form in which it is to-day.
Further, let me say that the Intercolonial never became a partner either in fact or in practice of the Canadian National system. Under an order in council it is true that the directors of the Canadian National Railway Company were appointed to administer the Intercolonial railway, always subject to the government as the railway board of directors were subject to the government. In that way the government never lost its hold upon the Intercolonial railway. But to-day we are transferring all our rights, placing absolute power in the board of trustees; no, not the board but only one member of that board because, if he is not satisfied with the decision of his intermittent colleagues on the board, he can veto their decisions and do as he pleases. He has the power to lease. What do we in the maritimes fear under that power? For years and years the Canadian Pacific has been looking for running rights over a part of the Intercolonial and a subsidiary of it from Saint John to Halifax. The Canadian Pacific Railway in 1929 demanded from the railway commissioners under the Railway Act that all freight originating east of Moncton and destined to points in the west touched by the Canadian Pacific, should be handed over to that railway at Saint John. That case was fought out with the result that while they did not succeed in having Saint John as the point of transfer, they did succeed in having Ste. Rosalie junction as the point at which the Canadian National would have to transfer its freight destined to points in the west touched by the Canadian Pacific. You talk of undue competition on the part of the Canadian National Railways as against the Canadian Pacific. What could you call that

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Veniot
attempt to grasp from the government railway freight that originated in its own district and at points distant hundreds of miles from the Canadian Pacific? What I fear and what many more people in the maritime provinces fear-and I think we are justified in having that fear-is -that this board of trustees, having the power to lease, may be induced to lease that part of the Intercolonial from Saint John to Halifax. Then what will happen? All freight originating east of Moncton including Prince Edward Island, will be carried over the lines leased to the Canadian Pacific via Saint John and on to the west, and that part of the Intercolonial railway, the location of which was made at the demand of the home government for strategic purposes, will be nothing but a branch line from Moncton to a point known as Levis on the river St. Lawrence and perhaps further on to Ste. Rosalie junction. What will become of the pledge of confederation under which the maritime provinces entered the union? What will become of the interests of the maritime provinces? If such a change arises-and I say it can arise and there is nothing under this measure to prevent it-not only will it make of the northern section from Moncton to Levis or Ste. Rosalie junction a branch line, but it will close out every bit of the work at Moncton, a city that has become one of the finest in the Dominion of Canada, a city that has prospered and been the centre of railway repairs, construction of locomotives and so on for the last thirty or forty years. The doors of that place will be closed and hundreds upon hundreds, yes, thousands of men will be thrown out of employment because, since we shall have to look after only the northern section of the old Intercolonial, it will not be necessary to keep those machine shops going any longer.

I wish at this point to make a suggestion to the minister and I feel I need not plead with members from the maritimes on both sides of the house. I know they understand the situation and they will use whatever influence they have to induce the government not to allow this matter to proceed as I have shown it may. I am going to suggest to the minister the following:
Notwithstanding anything in this act contained the board of trustees shall not lease,
or formulate any policy affecting the Intercolonial railway, without first submitting same to the consideration and approval of the governor general in council.
That is a rough draft, but it may be put in better shape. In order to allay the uneasiness which prevails in the maritime provinces I would ask the government to consider this proposition seriously and see if it is not possible for them, when the bill is in committee, to introduce an amendment to this effect.
I have just one or two other remarks to make and I hope the house will grant me the indulgence of listening to me although I hate to go beyond the limit of time. I have already referred to the board of trustees and their powers. I cannot support that clause in the bill; in fact, on that account I may be driven to vote against the measure on its second reading; but if I am driven to do so, nevertheless I wish it to be understood that I agree with the object of the bill in attempting to bring about such economies as will once more place the Canadian National Railways on a proper basis.
In connection with the arbitral tribunal I am irrevocably and unalterably opposed to any coercion. Coercion is not a democratic principle ; it should find no place in any legislation of this house. The railways have in the last two years by voluntary cooperation saved millions of dollars. The minister has told us that the Intercolonial alone has saved us, I think, 844,000,000 in the last year or so.

we should be so pessimistic about the railway situation. The Prime Minister, however, in his speech was very pessimistic, and right on top of preaching the pessimism he did he suggested that it might be necessary in the near future to have a plebiscite on amalgamation. I hope that the Prime Minister's pessimism when he denounced the railway situation was not preparatory to placing the principle of amalgamation before the people of Canada.
Mr. E. C. ST-PERE (Hochelaga) (Translation) : Mr. Speaker, the crisis through which we are passing embraces among other economic and social disturbances which it has brought about one known as the Canadian railway dilemma. Popular clamour, protests from various important corporations and demands of boards of trade induced the government about a year ago to refer this so important question of the national railways to a royal commission. I regret that such a question should have been submitted to a commission of men who are not responsible to the government of this country, instead of being referred to a special select committee of the house.
Within the last few years it seems to be a foregone conclusion that such commissions have always a set political purpose in that they relieve the government of responsibilities incumbent on them and afford an opportunity to party politicians to burden such a commission-appointed to study or administer certain public services-with the sins of omission or commission chargeable to the government when the reckoning day arrives.
The royal commission undertook the study of a difficult problem and among the causes of our railway embarrassment it quotes the following:
The over-development of railways beyond the immediate needs of the country.
There is no need of making a deep study of the history of Canadian railways to discover that this over-development of railways, beyond the immediate needs of the country, was never prompted by our present requirements, let us, however, recognize the fact here in the house where we have to assume responsibilities, let us wisely admit it, this over-development must be attributed to the fact that certain large companies or corporations, with no intention of helping the country while operating the railways, took up this work because of the profits they would derive or for purely financial ends; it is now incumbent on us, we from the various provinces,
[Mr. Veniot.l
to foot the bill for the most pernicious of all these large undertakings.
We were told that the Canadian government of that period assumed a great burden. In order that the house may be well informed, let us remember that Quebec represented at the time-I am not playing politics-by Sir Lomer Gouin's government, had refused to endorse the liabilities of the Canadian Northern Railway and that to-day that province of which I am a representative, is called upon, as all other provinces are, to foot the bill of our national railways. We are in Quebec at times too reticent in expressing our views on practical matters. Notwithstanding the fact that it had refused to participate in this huge expenditure and that it is forced to-day to contribute like others to the national deficit, Quebec was always the worse treated when it was a question of railway favours. Help was long in forthcoming.
The report further states:
Aggressive and uncontrolled competition between two nation-wide railway enterprises, a competitor the more disastrous in that one of the competitors was publicly-owned and supported by the full resources of the dominion.
I wonder whether by emphasizing the words "supported by the full resources of the Dominion," it would be possible to have this parliament adopt a bill which to my mind, would be equivalent to a merger in the near future of our Canadian railways. This uncontrolled 'competition between all railway companies became so evident on the other side of the line among the two hundred railways which span the country in all directions, that the United States railways themselves applied for permission from the Inter-State Commerce Commission not to merge but to be consolidated into four main railway systems which are not at present a burden to the country like ours are, but which nevertheless are a burden to the bondholders of these railway companies.
The Esch-Cummings Act allowed these railways to consolidate, however, what is most strange, is that the only trouble which arose came from Mr. Loree, president of the Delaware and Hudson Railway Company, and a member of the royal commission which the government appointed to study the problems of our railway systems. Further the report states:
The reactions of the world trade repression which began in 1929 and has progressively increased m its severity with each succeeding year.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. St-Pere
The commission wished to convey thereby that the international system of cooperation that we have always advocated, we the Liberal party in the house is, properly speaking, the only means of solving the present problem.
Again further the report states:
Competitions from other forms of transport, notably road transport.
Those who have studied the competition being waged between transportation companies will be very glad to leam what General Atterbury, president of the Pennsylvania Central had to say on this subject, on December 18, 1932. I shall read the English text so that my compatriots who are all versed in that language, will dispense with me translating it and also that my English speaking colleagues be immediately apprised of the views of General Atterbury who, as we are all aware, carries much weight.
"I believe," he said, "that the motor bus can and should be coordinated with the railroad to the mutual advantage of both and wth benefit to the public.
"Operated in a service supplementary to that of the railroad, it has a real place in the transportation of the future. It will replace unrcmunerative local trains, serve as a feeder of the railroads and speed up through service by making possible the elimination of numerous stops by long distance trains. Our company ha9 already begun to put this into actual practice by taking a financial interest in bus lines and coordinating their service with our train schedules. We have found these bus lines to be paying investments.
"We are doing the same thing in trucking. Motor transportation is best adapted for short hauls, railroad transportation for long hauls. We are using trucks in place of local freight trains and already freight is being moved direct from shipper to receiver without rehandling, through the use of detachable truck bodies hauled by motor to the railroad at the point of origin and again by motor from the railroad at the point of destination.
"We can carry the loaded truck body from city to city by rail for much less than it costs the trucker to move it over the highway. If the railroads act intelligently they will give to the motor industry their terminal deliveries and the motor industry in turn will find it the part of intelligence to give to the railroads the long hauls."
As one may note, this problem of road transport competition can be solved.
Inelasticity of freight rates and railway practice generally which prevents prompt action in the meeting of falling revenues and dealing effectively with competition from other forms of transport.
As we are all aware, sir, the question of freight rates is under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission of Canada. Did the commission which held the inquiry, in pointing out this new cause of the present railway embarrassment, wish to convey to us
that we should amend the Railway Commission Act?
The sixth cause mentioned in the royal commission's report reads as follows:
Contractural arrangements with labour organizations which set up a rigid wage scale and inflexible labour practices generally.
Residing in a county where a large part of the population depend for a livelihood on our railways, may I especially refer to this question. Railway employees were in the past looked upon as the aristocrats of the working classes, however, I wish to state that, within the last few years, they do not deserve this cognomen. During the present crisis, their wages were reduced and the number of those who were suspended is very considerable. First, allow me to quote from United States railway statistics. In 1926, there were in the LTrited States 1,801,180 railway men drawing in wages $2,990,441,936, namely, an average yearly salary for each, of $1,656. In 1929, the number of employees was reduced to 1,686,789 and their total wages amounted to $2,941,000,000. In 1931, the number of employees was reduced to 1,285,000 and wages to $2,150,000,000.
At the recent Chicago conference, where American and Canadian delegates were present, another cut in wages amounting to $210,000,000 was agreed upon. With reference to Canadian railway men may I quote from statistical records which I have just received this morning from the Bureau of Statistics: the largest number of employees registered, in June, 1929, was 201,056, and the number of those at present working on our railways decreased by 90,127 in 1932.
We can therefore state that the situation of railway employees is at present more than critical.
Are we going by a systematic reduction of expenditures to throw out of employment a larger number of men whose wages contribute to the city's welfare in the various sections of Montreal as well as in other cities of Canada.
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Hear, hear.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	Are we going to destroy, through an exaggerated and systematic reduction of expenditures in various services in order to solve this abnormal problem, the purchasing power of our workmen?
The railway men have addressed to parliament and to each member of the house a memorandum requesting an equitable representation in all services of the Canadian

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. St-Pere
National Railways and in all arbitration tribunals should this bill be enacted, a just and equitable representation of their various organizations. I approve, without restriction, of this memorandum.
I approve of it because it is couched in moderate terms and contains, in my humble opinion, fair distributive measures. One may object, that those suffering hardships in other industries are not given the same advantage to address to parliament requests which they consider just and reasonable. That is, sir, a deplorable fact. In principle, I am a unionist.
If our people insisted on having measures of distributive justice, such as various workers' organizations worthy of that name, have, heretofore, put into practice, to-day, there would be less unemployed depending on the dole.
I cannot, sir, accept or vote in favour of the bill under consideration. Part I is equivalent to the curtailment of certain constitutional rights; it also includes the privilege-more than a privilege-namely, the exclusive right of trustees not to submit to the house their budget. Our constitutional rights will only be recognized, according to this section of the bill, the day when this triumvirate acting as dictators will request parliament to foot the bill of the deficits which may result from their ignorance or poor railway management.
Part II of the bill contains the principle of co-opertion. It adds but little to the rights of the working classes. Very little consideration is given to the recommendations of labour unions and mention is hardly made of them, as we may judge by the following:
The national company, for and on behalf of itself and/or any or all other of the companies and other elements of which National railways as defined by this act is composed, and the Pacific company, for and on behalf of itself and/or any or all other of the companies and other elements, of which Pacific railways as defined by this act is composed, are, for the purposes of effecting economies and providing for more remunerative operation, directed to attempt forthwith to agree and continuously to endeavour to agree, and they respectively are, for and on behalf as aforesaid, authorized to agree, upon such cooperative measures, plans and arrangements as are fair and reasonable and best adapted (with due regard to equitable distribution of burden and advantage as between them) to effect such purposes. They are further directed that whenever they shall so agree they shall endeavour to provide, as part of such measure, plan or arrangement or otherwise, for a fair and reasonable apportionment as between the employees of National railways and Pacific railways, respectively, of such employment as may be incident to the operation of such measure, plan or arrangement.
[Mr. St-Pere.l
I think, sir, that instead of inserting in that section the words "to strive to include" the words "shall include" should have been inserted, so as to afford our railwaymen a further guarantee that their rights of seniority would be recognized. It is useless to further emphasize this point. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) who just preceded me in this debate has fully vindicated that right.
Part III of the bill, sir, constitutes a real danger for the constituency which I represent. As this riding includes railway headquarters and terminal stations were we to adhere to the decisions of this arbitral tribunal, our workers whose rights are in no way protected, would have no voice in the decisions arrived at with reference to the management of this department of the Canadian railways. Property owners who have built houses in the neighbourhood of terminal stations and who depend largely on the wages of railwaymen to meet the payments of mortgages and municipal taxes would find themselves, under the circumstances, unable to put in claims with the Railway Commission; at present, this is the only safeguard that their rights will be protected. This phase of the situation affects not only property owners located in this part of my riding but also merchants who depend on the purchasing powers of these workmen.
This clause in connection with enforced cooperation would give our railway companies a right to the granting of which I have always been opposed in the house: namely, the use in common of the Rouen. St. elevated line, as this would greatly depreciate the value of real estate in the Prefontaine ward.
When the people of Hochelaga elected me as their representative in this house, in 1921, my mandate was to use my own discretion in approving or disapproving of measures submitted to the house; however, one thing that I have not lost sight of, was that they gave me besides definite instructions to protect their private interests, when these were assailed in the house.
I shall close my remarks, sir, by this sound argument. This government can, without this act, reduce the expenditures of the National Railways by decreasing the number of directors. I have never had much confidence in the efficiency which the number of directors brought to the management of the Canadian National, ever since 1922; however, I request that the number of directors be more than three, and that the large Canadian labour organizations be represented.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. St-Pere
1 have no intention of suggesting any particular person to represent these labour organizations on the board of directors. I leave it to the discretion and wise co-operation of those who are at the head of these movements to choose their representatives.
Mr. Speaker, I shall vote against the second reading of this bill because I find in it no suggestion which can be formulated into a workable measure. I shall not support the measure because, as I mentioned a moment ago, the enactment of a number of its clauses would signify, for the constituency I represent and the section where I reside, a complete financial and economic disorganization.
We are sent to this parliament to legislate wisely, with a free mind. I should like to see this parliament adopt a measure allowing our railways to compete with one another, mot an exaggerated but a reasonable competition. Where are we to find this superman, this Chairman of the Board of Trustees which would apply, to the management of our national railways, this practical system which would relieve the present situation? The Atterburys, Harrimans, James J. Hills, Scullys, Van Severingens and others of such administrative ability are scarce in Canada. Why not leave the management to those who are, at present, at the head of our railways, to those officials of the Canadian Pacific who have been chosen by the board of directors, to those men of experience of the National Railway who, having started at the bottom of the ladder, have, to-day, climbed to the highest posts in our railways. The Grant Halls, Hungerfords, etc., notwithstanding what may he said to the contrary, have more experience, more practical knowledge of railway matters than those supposed experts that the government might appoint to manage the national railways. Are we going to brand as incompetent those who have grown up in this railway atmosphere, and have become, to-day, presidents or vice-presidents, after having started as call boys, yard foremen, etc.?' Let us discuss railways! Let us not give ourselves up to absurd notions, absolutely devoid of practical sense. Our railways must be managed by railway men. It does not behoove a lawyer, a doctor etc., without experience, even a great politician to substitute himself to those whom experience has formed and trained, who can solve the particular intricate and important problem of our Canadian railways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on the railway bill now before the house. I believe this is one of the most important bills that has come before this parliament, at any rate since I came here in the fall of 1930. I am glad in view of its importance that the bill has been discussed in a non-partisan way. I am, however, surprised at the attitude of some hon. members who seem to desire to dispose of it hastily. From what I have heard in the house I believe this bill means the end of public ownership of Canadian railways and the setting up of a new system in the conduct of railway affairs in Canada. If I am correct in that view then I think the house may well give ample time to the consideration of such a measure. It is not necessary for me to cover the ground already covered as to the history of the railways, the debt, and the coming into being of the present Canadian National Railways. That has been amply covered not only in this but in previous debates when railway matters were under consideration. But in connection with the debts of the railways I think it is hardly fair just to quote figures. We must not forget that the times when these railways were built were times of prosperity. They were the days of the development of our country. Surely some credit must be given for the development of this country of ours. I am frank to state, Mr. Speaker, that had the development of Canada been left to one railway, the Canadian Pacific, many districts that now are peopled would have remained undeveloped, and Canada would not have progressed to the extent she has. In passing I should also like to say that Canada, like no other country, relies almost entirely on railways and is dependent to quite a degree upon transportation. Our great wheat fields are farther from the seaboard than those of any other country. The average haul in the Argentine is 210 miles; in Australia 218 miles; in Russia 360 miles and in India, another great country, 550 miles. In Canada our wheat fields are about 900 miles from the central provinces to the east and from 600 to 700 miles from the western coast. As Mr. Hungerford has well said, we would have had no community growth in Canada without the railways. In the Canadian railways we have one of the finest and most efficient railway services in the world, and when I say the service is efficient I am not thinking particularly of the de luxe trains. I am thinking of the fast freight and passenger services that are given, and I venture to say that if it had been left to one 
railway, the Canadian Pacific, we would not to-day have been able to travel across the continent in some four and a half or five days; probably it would have remained at seven days. Mr. Beatty himself admitted that this efficiency was due to the competition of the Canadian National.
With regard to competition I should like to refer also to one remark made by Mr. Hungerford which I believe should be borne in mind. Addressing the Duff commission Mr. Hungerford said that competition in railway service in Canada affected only 25 per cent of the mileage, and that the remaining 75 per cent was non-competitive. I believe that should be taken into consideration indealing with this question. At page 953, immediately following Mr. Beatty, Lord Ash-field said that the competition of the Canadian National Railways had the effect of providing an unexcelled system of transportation for the Canadian people. It is true that the railways are not as prosperous as they should be or as we would like to see them, but what railways or what businesses are prosperous? The people themselves are not so prosperous. I think we all agree that what the railways need to-day is trade and tonnage. The lack of freight has contributed in large measure to the deficits shown by our railways, and in passing I might mention that the daily bulletin issued yesterday by the bureau of statistics states that freight traffic is about ten per cent less than it was in 1931. I do not think there is any question, Mr. Speaker, but that the lack of freight has brought about the problem with which we are now faced. I need only refer to the Duff commission, who said very plainly:
In so far as -the position of the Canadian railways is the result of the depression in world trade, they have merely shared the general fate of most industries and of railways in other countries. In the United States of America the recession in railway earnings did not appear until 1930, but by the end of 1931 the net operating income of the Class I roads had fallen from $1,395,348,471 to $662,314,465 (more than 50 per cent), which is greater than the reduction shown by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
If we had the trade of 1928 or 1929 I doubt if the present administration would have dared [DOT]to introduce the measure now under discussion. Advantage is being taken at the moment, I think-and I am only giving my own views- of the opportunity to eliminate- the competition of the Canadian National, not the competition of the Canadian Pacific. As Mr. Beatty said in outlining his proposals, the only alternative to those proposals was com-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Reid
petition, but Lord Ashfield stated that if you secure advantage through cooperation you eliminate competition. There are various kinds of competition, Mr. Speaker, and I believe the competition we have had in Canada with one privately owned and one publicly owned railway has proved to be the ideal system. It prevents a private corporation from securing a full monopoly, and that applies to the state as well. The one railway in competition with the other has been said by leading railway men throughout the world to be the ideal system for a country such as Canada.
We hear a great deal with regard to competition from trucks and ships. I would like to state in passing, Mr. Speaker, that we should take more interest in the competition from ships on canals. We have spent hundreds of millions of dollars in developing the canals which are used by ships from all over the world, which do not pay any toll for the use of those facilities. The trucks I realize present serious competition, but at least they contribute something to the revenues of our country. If hon. members would look up the amount of freight transported on the canals they would realize that this competition is more serious to the railways than is the competition from trucks. The other night the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) quoted the figures; he stated that the tonnage carried on the canals had increased almost in proportion to the decrease on our railways. This competition, as I say, should be noted, because it is making serious inroads on much of the traffic which could be handled by our railways. In spite of the fact that the country has spent millions of dollars in the development of the canal system these ships do not pay anything for the use of these trade routes or waterways.
In passing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to voice a little criticism of the St. Lawrence waterway proposal. I do not believe this should be proceeded with at this time, because in my opinion it would only provide more competition and less trade for the railways, and further we do not require more electrical power at present than is supplied by existing services. I believe that it would be wrong to go ahead with that project at this time, and I think the government would be well advised seriously to consider this matter. When we speak of the money that has been spent not only in constructing but also in purchasing railways it would be well for hon. members to look at the money that has been spent on the canals of this country. Many of those expenditures were just as foolish and in many cases just as tragic as some of the expenditures made on railway lines.
For a few moments now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with some of the speeches made by Mr. Beatty, not only those made before the Duff commission but also those made since the bill was introduced in the Senate. I should like to draw this to the attention of the house:
First of all, however, I would say that in my opinion the present bill is based on what I would call the Beatty and the Thornton proposals; it is almost along precisely the same lines as a bill that was presented by Mr. Ruel and Sir Henry Thornton.
With reference to Mr. Beatty, I would like to discuss for a moment his attitude towards one section of the bill, namely, with regard to the tribunal. It does seem strange to me that he should travel throughout the length and breadth of the country speaking against the setting up of this arbitral tribunal, because when he appeared before the Duff commission he seemed to be, and as a matter of fact was, I believe, in favour of it. At page 955 Lord Ashfield asked Mr. Beatty whether he thought the tribunal should deal with services and rates or whether there should be two separate tribunals. Mr. Beatty replied that it was immaterial so long as the tribunal was properly constituted. Then Sir Joseph Flavelle asked him this question: If a separate board was set up, should it be named by the government, and his answer was yes. Sir Joseph Flavelle then said-and this is very important-that Mr. Beatty's suggestion would mean one system of railways in Canada for all time to come. Now the more I think of this bill, the more I hear it discussed, and the more I delve into the proceedings of the Duff commission, the more firmly convinced I am that the bill is the beginning of one railway system in Canada for all time to come. Just what Mr. Beatty's idea was in going throughout the length and breadth of the country opposing the tribunal, after discussing it and practically approving it before the Duff commission, I am not at all sure. Personally I believe that there are one or two reasons for his doing so. For one thing, I believe that the opposing of the tribunal publicly by Mr. Beatty was just so much eyewash. He knew or believed that the government was going to set up a tribunal. It had been previously discussed, and he probably thought that if he opposed this publicly the people would think that there was some good in the tribunal and so parliament would adopt it without much opposition. The other reason, I believe, was this. He probably thought that his opposition
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Reid

would serve as a sort of smoke screen for something else contained in the bill.
I refer to part I of the bill, which I think is the most important part of it, because it deals with the three trustees. It deals with the setting up of the board of trustees, the powers of the men who compose the board, how they are to deal with the Canadian National Railways, and so on, and that I am convinced is the most important part of the whole arrangement with regard to the handling of the Canadian National system. I believe it was Christ who said, with reference to the ten commandments about which he had been speaking:
On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
I would say that on this part of the bill hang all the law and the prophets, but I would spell prophets "profits." Let us examine what part I provides in regard to the trustees. Subsection 2 of section 4, under Part I, provides:
One of such trustees shall be their chairman. He shall devote his whole time to performance of the duties of his office, and shall not be an officer of any company other than a company which is comprised in national railways, and shall not during his tenure of office as trustee become a director of any company other than a company which is comprised in national railways of which he was not a director at the time of his appointment.
That is a wise proviso, that the chairman shall not be associated with any other railway than the Canadian National system. But it is different with the other two; there is nothing in the bill to ensure the appointment of one or the remaining two trustees who, if not connected with the Canadian Pacific Railway or some other railway, might be more sympathetic to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I suggest now to the government in all seriousness that there should be a provision to the effect that no trustee shall be in any way connected with the Canadian Pacific nor shall have any stock or shares in that company, because I cannot help thinking that when men have invested a considerable sum of money in stocks and bonds one must naturally say of them, what the old book says, that where their treasure is there will their heart be also.
I realize that it is difficult at this late stage of the debate to introduce any new point, or anything that has not been already covered, but I would like to deal for a few moments with some other phases of the bill, and in this connection I would point out that the bill follows quite closely the recommendations of the Duff commission report except

in one particular. I was interested to hear the Minister of Railways, in reply to an hon. member who was speaking, make the statement about something in the bill, to which reference had been made, that it was in accordance with the recommendations of the commission. Well, when they were following out the recommendations of the commission I am surprised that they did not follow them all, because one of the recommendations, with regard to the powers of the arbitral tribunal, reads, at page 66:
The powers of the arbitral tribunal shall be Capable of being invoked by either railway or by the dominion or any provincial government.
I believe that in omitting this recommendation the bill leaves out one of the most important recommendations of the commission, in fact the only remaining link between the railways and the people of Canada, through either the Dominion government or the provincial governments. I cannot help thinking that if the bill passes in its present form-and that is how we must view it at the moment-the control of the railways belonging to the people of Canada will be gone forever, and public ownership in the Canadian National Railways will then be at an end.
Let us examine, however, this recommendation carefully, and frankly, I am opposed to dictatorship in any form, whether in railways or government or business or anything else; I am absolutely opposed to the principle of a dictator. When the commission deemed it wise to insert that provision which I have just read, I suggest that the government should seriously consider putting that clause into the bill, so as to leave some power to the government, either provincial or federal. If that were done, in the event of things not working out right, or in the event of any injustice being done the people, then the people could come to the government and ask that they be heard. Almost every other suggestion made by the Duff commission has been followed; read the bill through and you will see that almost in toto the conclusions set forth in the report have been followed. You will find provisions with regard to budget, annual report to parliament, audit, cooperation between the railways, constitution of the arbitral tribunal, and so forth. Every one of them is embodied in the bill, but when you come to the suggestion that the powers of the arbitral tribunal should be capable of being invoked by either railway or by the dominion or any provincial government, you find this highly important recommendation omitted, leaving entirely to the railways the sole right of appeal.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Reid
Is there any reason at all why the people of this country should be debarred from being heard? If the bill passes in its present form there will be no use in their coming to parliament because parliament will be dissociated from railway matters entirely. In fact, I do not believe that we shall need a Minister of Railways after this bill goes through; his duties will be very much lighter than they are at the present time at any rate. His activities would be much less than they are at the present time because the three trustees would handle the operation of the entire Canadian National railway system.
How' will this political tribunal work out in practice? What will happen when both railways agree to abandon, say one hundred miles of main line or other track? In case of agreement the arbitral tribunal will not of course be consulted, the abandonment will simply be put into effect. If one railway suggests to the other that a certain line of track should be cut off and the other railway does not agree, then it -will come before the tribunal where it will be left to one man to decide. What of the people affected? What of the towns which will have to be abandoned? They will have no right to come to parliament and be heard if this bill passes in its present form. The most important clause of all, and the one which would enable them to be heard, has been left out, the only clause which would have provided a link or connection between the people and this parliament. I maintain that such an omission is very serious. I might state that Mr. Beatty proposed that five thousand miles of track could be abandoned while Mr. Loree thought that ten thousand miles could be abandoned.
Are hon. members fully aware that Mr. Beatty stated that an agreement had been arrived at between the officers of both companies to the effect that 1,582 miles of line should be abandoned? If hon. members will read the report they will see that such an agreement was arrived at. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways have both stated that this bill does not mean amalgamation, but if an agreement to abandon 1,582 miles of line has been arrived at, and carried into effect what else can it mean? Surely the government is not going to set up a dictatorship especially in the face of the statement by Mr. Beatty that it has been agreed to abandon 1,5S2 miles of line.
We have been told that we should treat this bill from a national and not from a sectional point of view. But when I see by the report that certain mileage in British Columbia is to be abandoned, and that the Port Mann shops near New Westminster need not
be used and that the elevator which I discussed the other night is also going to be sidetracked, and that the city of New Westminster will also be isolated, can I be blamed for rising and protesting against this bill? After all, can we entirely dissociate sectionalism from our debate? Are we not elected on sectionalism? I believe that I was elected primarily to represent the people in the constituency of New Westminster and so must look after their interests; therefore I am taking strong exception to the bill.
For the remaining few moments I should like to deal with what may be expected to take place in British Columbia should this bill pass in its present form. In case the Minister of Railways takes exception I may assure him ll cannot speak for the whole of British Columbia, but I shall speak only for my own constituency. If the recommendations of the report are carried out, my section of the country will be affected. I should like first of all to go back into the railway history of British Columbia. Before entering confederation, British Columbia was promised a railway, but it was necessary for that province to send a man to London to interview Queen Victoria before the then Dominion government would come through. The Canadian Pacific was then induced to construct a line through to British Columbia. Although a very excellent route had been chosen by the government they decided to take a shorter but more difficult route through to the coast. They constructed their line through Kicking Horse pass instead of through Yellowhead pass which is some 1,600 feet lower. After completion the Canadian Pacific adopted a very high attitude in connection with freight rates and so in 1910, the people of British Columbia having raised such an agitation against the Canadian Pacific Railway, the government of that day-I believe Sir Richard McBride was premier-decided that it would be wise to have another railroad in competition with and to hold down the Canadian Pacific, and so the Canadian Northern was constructed. Certain guarantees were given by the province which, as the Prime Minister has said, were taken over by the dominion but I believe that we lost considerably by the Dominion government taking over these guarantees. The government of British Columbia intended to use this railroad as a lever against the Canadian Pacific and as a competitor and so they enacted legislation that they the province were to have full control over the regulation of freight rates. When the railway was completed it was taken over by the Dominion government, and the provincial government lost that control



C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Reid
and had no further powers or rights to regulate rates. Freight rates were then put under the Board of Railway Commissioners and so we were still under the domination of the Canadian Pacific. That company always argued against a reduction in freight rates and although British Columbia has protested since that time that company's rates has always been used as the yardstick in the discussion of freight rates, about which British Columbia has spent many thousands of dollars.
The Canadian Northern was built over one of the best grades in the Dominion of Canada. It runs over a low water level grade of some four-tenths of one per cent as against the grade of the Canadian Pacific which is as high as two and a half per cent in many places. In hauling wheat from the prairies to Vancouver, one engine on the Canadian Northern can draw three times as many cars as a similar engine on the Canadian Pacific. The same thing applies with trains coming east from Vancouver, either with empties or loaded cars. An engine coming from Vancouver to Edmonton via the Yellowhead pass can draw three times as many cars as an engine on the Canadian Pacific from Vancouver to Calgary via the Kicking Horse pass.
It is now proposed, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Pacific obtain the use of the best grade through the mountains, and according to the proposals made all traffic from the east shall go over their line from a point seventy-nine miles out from the city of Vancouver. Similarly, all the traffic from the orient, Great Britain or any country will use the Canadian Pacific tracks and terminals and run over the Canadian Pacific line as far as Hope and then branch over to the Canadian National. In my opinion the Canadian Pacific is having the best of it all the way through; it is a case of heads I win, tails you lose. What effect will this have on the territory to be abandoned? As I have stated, the Canadian National has a terminal at Port Mann. No doubt Senator McRae will be glad to see this terminal discarded because it must still be a thorn in his flesh since he got out of the scheme from which I am told he made a considerable amount of money.
Then there are the yards and ships where between 400 and 600 men will in all probability be let out. The city of New Westminster will have no railway connection. It is true that a little branch goes from there to the main line, but perhaps this will also be lifted. Then there is the elevator which was built and has close connection with the Canadian National Railway. In the abandonment of that seventy-nine miles of track, the
IMr. Reid.]
cities and towns in the territory all the way down will be left stranded. All wheat and grain products coming from the prairies will first of all have to go into the city of Vancouver and then out again to the Fraser valley. This will add considerable more to the cost of production on the part of dairymen and poultrymen in that district. The situation is almost too serious to contemplate. Hon. members should go down and read the report and then I think they will agree with me that the proper stand to take is to vote against this bill on its second reading. It is all very well to say: We shall vote for the principle and then we shall make changes in committee. But what is the principle of the bill? I think it is evident to the house now that it will ultimately mean amalgamation if it does not mean that now. It is true that the Prime Minister has told us that the bill does not amalgamate the railways, but in a year or two that is I believe what will occur. The Canadian Pacific will then control all the traffic going into Vancouver from seventy-five miles out and they are going to abandon tracks throughout Canada. In going through the report I notice that the Canadian Pacific were to get the best of the deal all the way through. It was the poorly paying sections of railway that the Canadian Pacific were to abandon and all the best paying portions the Canadian Pacific are proposing to be taken over and controlled by them.
I protest very seriously against this being done. I intend to vote against the second reading of the bill and I ask all hon. members to read, as I have, the statements which were made before the Duff commission. I believe those who are interested and who have sections that are going to be abandoned will act and vote against the bill the same as I intend to do.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCO IS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to thank the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) for what he said the other day, as follows:

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Pouliot
The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Haekett) said that the government should be [DOT]supported at all costs. These are his words:
These are times when I believe a government should be upheld, steadied and supported, almost at any cost.
It is a very good thing that the hon. gentleman is not Minister of Railways and I understand the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) told him that he was sorry he should speak in that way. Our motto should be: "Salus populi suprema lex." The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) said on another occasion:

As I do not intend to have any cause for regret, I shall vote against the bill.
One has indeed a high regard for most of the commissioners, but who represented the good city of Toronto and the business men of Ontario? These are the words of the Prime Minister:
Certainly Sir Joseph Flavelle will, by the common consent of all who know him, be regarded as one of the foremost business men this country has yet produced.
He was one of the commissioners. Was he the expert who told the Prime Minister that Canada has potentialities for the production of 8,500,000 hogs by 1937, and 10,000,000 by 1942? This is the question: Was he selected to look after any possibilities of trade in hogs?
Owing to the fact that every section of tne bill is to be scrutinized while we are in committee, I now intend to discuss two matters which are so closely related to the railway problem that it depends upon them for its solution. First is unemployment in its relation to the railway problem. The other day the Prime Minister said:
Human interest centres in the employees of the system only if it continues to operate, for if it does not operate there is no employment, and unless a very, very great improvement is made in conditions the system as a whole cannot continue to operate.
Later, he spoke about "default certain and positive for at least some period of time." He used the language that he used when he was leader of the opposition to paint the conditions of the country; he was painting them with a black brush. The picture is a rather gloomy one. Would it not have been apropos for him to add: "We have succeeded where others have failed." On Thursday last he [DOT]said also:
I feel that the magnitude of the problem that confronts this parliament is little understood or appreciated.
