This is not very complimentary to the Canadian people. The hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), when he spoke in this debate, said:
The Minister of Railways claimed that the railway problem was the most important problem that we have to face at this particular time. I do not agree. I think that the greatest problem in this dominion that we have got to face at this time is the unemployment problem that is now before parliament.
An hon. member interjected:
Both problems are connected.
Mr. Heaps: I am quite ready to admit that there is a connection between the two.
What has been done with regard to unemployment relief? On September 16, 1930, the Prime Minister said:
Our tariff measure is not a general revision of the tariff, but deals only with such items in the tariff as it is believed will ensure additional employment to a large number of men and
women in Canada	 We have very definite
assurances from the producers in this country that as a result of the action we are taking they will increase the number of men and women in their mills and factories.
Such was the expectation in 1930. At that time the total number of unemployed was 107,000. To-day the total number of men, women and children on direct relief is 1,357,562. Such is the failure in 1933. An hon. member said on February 24:
Does that include all unemployed?
Mr. Deputy Speaker: All such questions can be properly asked in committee.
With regard to unemployment may I quote what was said by the ex-Minister of Labour as reported on page 2823 of Hansard of March 8:
I have also in mind the fact that several towns along one of those lines are railroad terminals, with populations consisting chiefly of railroad employees. We built and developed our railroads, as I say, by authority of the parliament of Canada. Young men left the farms and other occupations and entered the railroad service; they were sent out to these isolated places in order to serve the people of Canada. They got married, built their little homes, their churches, schools and community halls, and now with one stroke of the pen it is intended, as I regard it, to throw these people with their wives and children and dependents into the discard.
Mr. Manion: May I offer a suggestion to my hon. friend, with all respect? He is making a lot of positive statements about what is going to happen under the bill, regarding which no one knows the outcome in the end at all.
Note that, Mr. Speaker, "regarding which no one knows the outcome in the end at all." The minister goes on to say:
I doubt if it is wise to throw the fear of that sort of thing into a lot of people at least until there is more cause than there is at present.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Pouliot
do now is reduce the tariff to normalcy, and unless he does it at once no successful railway legislation can be enacted. Therefore is not Bill A of the Senate premature and untimely?
I have, sir, a very strong objection to the bill being submitted to committee of the whole house, because the minister did not think it necessary to go to the trouble and expense of hearing the witnesses over again. The hon. gentleman said:
... it is my opinion that it is not necessary to go to the. trouble and expense of hearing these witnesses over again.
First I would say that the matter of expense is only a pretext. What was the expense of hearing witnesses in the Senate? Does the minister know? Will he tell us? Was it so much? The railway debt is $2,300,000,000 a figure which "might be almost unbelievable because the aggregate is so large" according to the Prime Minister's own words. Most ridiculous! What would be a few thousand dollars of expense compared with such a formidable figure as that of the debt of the railways? If it is true that the primary duty of the house is to legislate, every member has the unquestionable right to hear any witness in order to be familiar with the facts, and all the facts, before he passes judgment on them, even if this bill is a temporary measure. Therefore I not only oppose the bill; I also oppose the motion of the minister to refer it to the committee of the whole. I am sorry to oppose the legislation introduced by the minister, but I am sure it is not exactly his legislation; I think it has been imposed upon him.
The second reason why this bill is not referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines is the fear of the government that trouble will follow. At pages 1875 and 1898 of Hansard I find that although t!he press of the country reported last fall that the Canadian Pacific had bought Dominion bonds to the value of $2,000,000, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) pointed out twice on February 7 last that that company did not even indirectly subscribe to a single bond. How could that mystery be solved unless the Canadian Pacific officials and the press reporters were called as witnesses before a committee. There is much more in that. On February 7 an Italian bond issue of $51,000,000 was oversubscribed in one day, but it took weeks to subscribe the Canadian loan last fall. Why? The Canadian people have no more confidence in the leader of the government, and this is the writing on the wall. Internal trade is much less for that reason, and the railways suffer severely as a result.
fMr Pouliot.]
I suggest that there is extravagance in the administration of the railway, Mr. Speaker. On October 17 I placed a question on Hansard, which appears at page 251. The question, which was No. 22 was struck out, so I should like to place it on record now:
1.	How many superintendents are there in the Canadian National Railways?
2.	How many assistant superintendents?
3.	How many special ears are at the disposal of the superintendents?
4.	Is each superintendent entitled to a special car for his own use?
5.	How many cooks or butlers are in charge of such private cars?
6.	What is the total annual salary paid to them?
7.	What is the total annual cost of:	(a)
food; (b) delicacies; (c) cigars and cigarettes, and (d) liquors and soft drinks paid for those special cars during the last three years?
8.	To what department of the railway are those expenses charged?
The same questions could be asked with regard to the Canadian Pacific railway. On October 17 the Prime Minister rose in his place and made a statement with regard to this question and another which was on the order paper at the same time. Before putting my questions on the order paper I took the precaution of communicating with the Minister of Railways, who had no objection to the questions. The Prime Minister said:
With respect to this question and other similar questions on the order paper, notably No. 22, it will be observed that the government is being asked questions regarding trie internal operation of a railway which it does not in any sense control for the purpose of offering answers to questions such as are asked. This question obviously, from the very language of it, would in any event have to stand as an order for return and the same might be said with regard to question 22. It is quite clear that to ask the government questions regarding matters that are under the control of the railways, for instance in regard to the facilities that are offered to their own servants to discharge their duties, is something that in my judgment cannot be fairly asked and the only answer that could be made would be: The government has no information. With that answer the hon. member will have to be content with respect to questions such as Nos. 19 and 22.
Then I wrote the assistant clerk of the House of Commons on October 24, as follows:
On October 17th instant (Hansard, p. 251), the right honourable Prime Minister made the following remarks about question No. 19: "This question obviously, from the very language of it, would in any event have to stand as an order for return and the same might be said with regard to question 22."
As those questions did not stand as orders for return, I herewith enclose motions to the same effect, in accordance with the Prime Minister's suggestion.
I hope that the attached motions will appear in the votes and proceedings of the day.
Please answer in writing.
Sincerely yours,
Jean-Franqois Pouliot.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Pouliot
The answer was as follows:
In reply to your letter of the 24th instant, enclosing motions that questions 19 and 22 (Hansard, p. 275) stand as orders for return, I am instructed by His Honour the Speaker to advise you that he considers the same were disposed of in the statement of the Prime Minister on OotobeT 17, which was as follows: "the only answer that could be made would be 'The government has no information!'"
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) Thos. M. Fraser, Clerk Assistant.
Since the Prime Minister runs both ways it is hard to follow him. The Prime Minister did not deign to answer. If hon. members look at Hansard for October 11 last, at pages 74, 75 and 76 they will find the facts with regard to the over-staffing of the Canadian National, and the same thing applies to the Canadian Pacific. One article of my railway policy is that wherever possible it is in the public interest to dispense with the services of one high salaried and useless official rather than four or more good employees. In the meantime a lot of idle officials keep their soft jobs while the heads of families are dismissed.
Before concluding my speech, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the superman idea is worn threadbare.' The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said:
.-the Canadian people ought to thank God that in these days of stress we have a superman.
This is not flattery or adulation; it is just a slight exaggeration. The Prime Minister, who perhaps conceals an inferiority complex behind a superiority complex, probably thought of this when two days later he said:
I recognize the fact that no soft words are going to solve this problem, and no criticism of high taxation will pay the bills that result from it.
Was the Prime Minister too shy to mention high tariff? No superman should be the leader of any government; the leader of a government should be human. If the Prime Minister is a superman why has the business of the country gone from bad to worse since he took office? The primary duties of a Prime Minister are many. On March 9 of this year the Prime Minister said:
These are times for plain speaking, and there is no hon. member now looking me in the face who does not know that what I say is true. I know it is as true as the fact that I am looking at hon. gentlemen opposite.
The other afternoon there was an interesting argument with regard to the primary duty of the House of Commons, but is it not high time that we enumerated the primary and elementary duties of a Prime Minister? I conceive them to be as follows: first, not to
allow anyone to bum incense under his nose and call him a superman; second, to attend the sittings of the house of which he is the leader, or to resign if he cannot do so; third, to think before any legislation, orders in council or otherwise, is passed, in order not to have to repeal it later on.
I have very little time left, Mr. Speaker, and since my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) in his eloquent speech yesterday made reference to the utterances of the Prime Minister with regard to Sir Wilfrid Laurier I will only touch on that matter in passing. The Prime Minister blamed Sir Wilfrid Laurier for our railway problem, and here is what the right hon. gentleman said in my home town, Riviere du Loup, during the last election campaign:
Air. Bennett drew cries of "shame" from the audience when he contrasted Premier Mackenzie King with Laurier. When the United States had threatened to cut Canada off bonding privileges Laurier had declared that Canada would build two railways of her own. But when protection was asked against American imports Air. King had said, "Hush, do not provoke the United States."
At that time Mr. King was Prime Minister and Mr. Bennett was leader of the opposition, so he had to say something disagreeable. No one has forgotten the speech delivered by the Prime Minister on November 30 last, during the course of which he invoked the memory of Laurier, the father of our country, no less than thirty times in order to excuse all the wrongs brought about by his nefarious policy of high tariff. So I think his reference to Laurier last Thursday could be described in Horace's four words, Minxerit in patrios cineres.
Thanks to the strenuous battle conducted by the Liberal party last fall the eyes of the Canadian people are open. They see the humbug of the trade agreements that were signed at the Ottawa conference, and the efforts of our party have been supported by the subsequent recommendation of the president of the Canadian Bankers' Association, backed by all the banks, that the tariff should be lowered. Our case is just as good to-day as it was then. We are fighting for our principles and for the public good; if the supporters of the government do not understand this, at least it is well known to the Canadian people.
Now I have two suggestions to make, and if they are not welcomed by the government as a whole I hope at least they will be received by the Minister of Railways. My first suggestion is that we should not increase the number of unemployed, and my second suggestion is that the tariff should be lowered to a normal height. We are living in times

of stress, and this is not the time for beating drums. Every man must be judged by his accomplishments, and when a man is incompetent, whether he be a prime minister or a janitor, he must get. out. We must not make a farce of things. The future of the nation is at stake and I am tired of all the incenseburning and the drum-beating when the business of the country, the strength of the nation, is going to the dogs. Let us put a stop to it. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it not possible, instead of having a union government, for all men of good will to join together to expel from any position those who are unworthy of it because of incompetence?

I wish to join with others in complimenting the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) on the speed'- he made in introducing the bill, and on ms plea that the discussion should be non-partisan and without prejudice. May I say that if I myself were a minister in the government and had a bill before the house I too would make a very strong plea to all members of the opposition to be patriotic and non-partisan, and would ask them to put my bill through without too much discussion and without prejudice.
The minister says that there is in this bill nothing that is to conflict with the platform of "amalgamation never", and I think it is a fortunate thing for the country that it has the assurance of the Prime Minister that he is going to insert a special clause in the bill which will make amalgamation impossible. The whole purpose of the bill is to join together certain services, to amalgamate; and how the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways is going to bring about amalgamation without amalgamation is something I shall be interested in watching.
Like many other members who have spoken, I am quite in agreement with the suggestion that the president of the railway should not at the same time be chairman. I am quite in agreement that there is considerable room for improvement in the method adopted in the past in financing the railway. I am also in agreement that much can be accomplished in changing the method of auditing and to carry on a continuous audit. After I have stated my agreement in these particulars I must say that, even including the economy which is supposed to be the basis of the whole measure, I am opposed to practically every other clause in the bill.
The various ramifications of the bill are stated in legal verbiage. For my own purposes I have put in the language that we employ every day, my view of it. The bill provides
iMr. Pouiiot.]
for the abdication of all governmental control and all governmental responsibility in connection with the railways, to be placed in the absolute control of one man to be called the chairman of trustees, with full power to do as he wills, without restraint.
The first, section provides for three trustees, two of whom have no authority whatever. Although these two trustees may be and are permitted to vote, their vote, or any other action, shall be without effect. The other trustees shall be the chairman, who shall iiave absolute authority in all things in connection with the national railways, without responsibility to anyone or to the government.
The governor in council will make the original appointments of trustees, and subsequent vacancies may be filled from a panel submitted by a committee, in which committee the present Conservative government have full confidence. This committee is expected to submit only such names for appointment as would continue in these offices the Conservative dynasty, regardless of what political party may be in power in Canada.
The absolute authority of the chairman of trustees will permit him, without any restraint whatever from the government or anyone else, to sell, lease, amalgamate or manipulate in any way the whole or any portion of the assets of the national company.
His authority will enable him to release or discharge, without restraint, any or all of the employees of the national company.
When this bill was first brought before the house considerable credit was given the Duff commission for what it hatched out. It is unnecessary for me to refer again to the report of the committee on railways and shipping wherein this commission was suggested. The commission sat; it spent a considerable amount of the people's money going from one end of the country to the other; it drew up its report and handed it to the Minister of Railways, and we expected some originality in the report, as well as some originality from the Minister of Railways. Certainly we thought that the Prime Minister at any rate would as usual be original. We find however that as in most cases in the history of legislation on the part of the Conservative party, this bill has its precedent-the precedent to take from the people all control over that which the people own. It is a peculiar thing that the Conservative attitude of the present government is reflected in the report of the Conservative royal commission on railways and transportation in Canada; I am referring to what is known as the Drayton-Acworth

report. The commissioners of that body were Mr. A. H. Smith, Mr. (now Sir Henry) Drayton, and Mr. W. M. Acworth.

The trustees should be five in number. The first trustees should be named in the act of parliament constituting the board.
The tenure of office should be the same as that of judges of the supreme court,-
Now we know where the Prime Minister gets his fondness for supreme courts.
-with the exceptions hereafter noted. Three
trustees-

Three trustees, one of whom should be the chairman, should, if possible, be men of railway experience. Of the two remaining trustees, we think it would be desirable that one should be selected on the ground of business and financial experience, and the other as specially possessing the confidence of railway employees. They should not be expected to give their whole time.
Again we have repetition. The report continues:
Their maximum salary might be laid down in the act, to be adjusted later when the requirements of the position became evident. Every trustee on appointment should be required to divest himself of all interest in Canadian railway bonds or stock, and should further satisfy the appointing authority that he has no other interest that conflicts with his duties as trustee.
All appointments other than those of the original trustees should be for a fixed period of seven years,

-except that in the case of a casual vacancy, owing to death or disability or resignation, the appointee should hold office only for the remainder of the term for which the trustee whom he replaces was appointed.

That sounds familiar too.

obviously are unfit to have any place in Canadian life. "Public charge" is closely connected with professional begging. Under this clause a large number of people have been deported from Canada. I have the figures here for the fiscal years 1930-31, 1931-32 and up to September, 1932, giving a grand total for that two and a half years of 9,446 persons deported for becoming public charges. I have not the figures for the last five months; they were not available the other day, but I am informed that the proportion is about the same w'hich would bring the number up to 12,000 or 13,000 people deported on the ground of being public charges. In the twTo and a half years to which I have referred, 2,146 people were deported because of their having been convicted of criminal offences, and 458 because of misrepresentation or stealth. These, with those deported for other causes make a total in that two and a half years of 15,658 persons. It is obvious that with 12,000 or 13,000 people deported on the ground of their being public charges, the matter is rather serious. I am informed that a great many of those people were deported with their own consent. In fact I think the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) issued a statement not long ago in which he said that something like 46 per cent of the British deportees had made application to be deported; also that something like 6 per cent only of the British ordered to be deported had appealed, and about 14 per cent of the non-British. It does not seem to me that these latter proportions are very significant, for I think most people, once ordered deported, would hardly think it worth while to appeal, and would accept the deportation order without further protest. I am not in any way blaming the department for having deported this large number of people. As long as the law stands as it is and the phrase " public charge " is not clearly defined or definitely limited, it is quite within the authority of the minister to deport anyone who is in receipt of relief.
Further than that, I think we all recognize that in most cases the initiative in deportation proceedings has been taken by the various municipalities, which have found themselves carrying a tremendous burden in carrying the people coming on relief. Many of these have come in in comparatively recent years, and municipalities have said: " We cannot carry the burden; why not ship them out of the country?" I can quite understand the pressure that municipalities may put on the department, but I do not think that warrants us as a country in deporting people of this class. If people have shown that they

are criminals or professional beggars, or are not qualified to earn a living in normal times in this country, I think it is quite right that they should be deported. In fact they should never have been allowed inside our gates; there should have been stricter supervision to begin with. But we all recognize that at present we are in the midst of a great depression, that there are tens of thousands of our own native born Canadians who cannot get work to support themselves and have had to go on relief. That is no crime, and no indication that they are incapable of earning a living under normal conditions; it is their misfortune. It would seem to me that in such conditions we should carry immigrants of this class, just as we are trj'ing to carry our own native born Canadians.
I would recall what all members of the house know, that we spent millions upon millions of dollars to induce these people to come to this country, and I would also note that the greater number deported have been returned not to Europe but to the British Isles. We sent people to England and Scotland to tell what a grand country this was. I did not think it worth while to take up the time of the house in reading the glowing advertisements which were inserted in the English newspapers begging people to come to Canada and assuring them that they could make a good living in this country. Many of them took us at our word; they sold their little homes, disposed of most of their furniture, gave up their jobs and came out here. Some of them prospered when there was an opportunity for them to prosper, but when hard times came they were thrown out of employment with many native-born Canadians. Perhaps because they were not so deeply rooted in this country they were among the first to be thrown out of work, but that is no reason why we should try to evade our responsibility of caring for them during this time of depression. I am quite sure hon. members must have had individual eases brought to their attention. Very often when men were sent back to the old country their family ties were broken and their former occupations were gone, and there was a depression in their own country. Whether or not they would be able to establish any claim for relief; would depend upon the particular country. Under these circumstances it seems to me that wre should not continue this process of deporting people simply because they have had to accept relief. I think we might accomplish the purpose I have in mind by a definition of a public charge which would exclude this particular class of people from the operation of this act.

I do not say that they are whife collar jobs or anything of that sort, but these people are offered honest toil with a going rate of wage, and they refuse to take the work. In fact, I have received communications to the effect that they will not take the work because they have only to wait a short time until another party comes into power when they will not have to work at all. I can scarcely subscribe to that, but that is the feeling amongst them. In another city in Canada we have a similar condition, where our colonization field staff was requested by the authorities not to solicit for any more jobs for single men because they would not accept work at the current rate of wages. These men are malingerers, and if we restrict the effect of the language of the present section we simply divest the person who is administering the law of the power to take care of cases of that kind.

They were comparatively recent arrivals and they considered that if they were returned to the land of their origin they could be reunited with relatives or friends and could probably tide over this time better than they would amongst strangers. That is not a desire to which we could take exception, it is a very natural desire. The only method which this government can invoke generally is to return people to the land of their origin when they apply for deportation stating that they cannot get work. The resolution which I received from the church authorities in Toronto reads in part as follows:
From time to time this session has learned from newspapers and other sources of information, that the deportation of inhabitants of Canada to their respective countries of origin is proceeding on a large scale, at the rate of thousands of deportees per annum. The persons so dealt with are not only of foreign birth, but also from England, Scotland and other parts of Great Britain. This process is secret in its nature. No public trial, or trial of any kind, seems to be required, but at the discretion or caprice of some public official, men, women and children whose only crime is their poverty or illness, are haled away and sent overseas, in many cases without money, without proper clothing, and even without food.
Until recent years, it was the policy of every successive government in Canada to foster and encourage immigration, not from Britain only but from the countries of continental Europe. People of these countries, attracted by the highly coloured advertisements of Canada, its vast and varied resources, its cheap and fertile lands, came in numbers up to 400,000 or more per, annum. Much of this immigration has already been absorbed into Canadian life, and in industry, intelligence, and the essentials of citizenship, the newcomers have proven not inferior to the average of native born Canadians. Many of them have struggled hard and valiantly with the inevitable difficulties attending their efforts to establish a permanent footing. Some have failed, and in these distressing times are regarded as "likely to become a charge upon the public." Hence, they are ejected from the country to which they had been invited and in which they had hoped to find a home. Even an English widow, temporarily ill and out of work is, with her helpless children, driven off with the rest.
This session has no sympathy whatever with revolutionary or so-eailed communistic principles. but it is constrained to protest against this inhuman, wholesale and secret deportation, resembling in essence as it does the expulsion of the Greeks from Turkey after the great war, the activities of the Ogpu in Soviet Russia, or the historic carrying away of the people of Israel by their Assyrian coriquerors.

I am not suggesting that in levity; I think this is a matter for the serious consideration of every hon. member. Who is to judge of the mentality and the integrity of Napoleon and the motives that inspired him? Who is to judge of the motives that inspired Kaiser Wilhelm? There is no precedent by which we can judge those men. They were not subjected to the ordinary laws by which common individuals are judged. They were above the law, above restraint; they were men who invariably felt called upon by the Great Ruler of the universe, men who had a vision, who had to take the people along a certain course whether they would or not. They said: The people must go to my goal, not to their own; the people do not always know what is best for them. So sometimes we have before us a Napoleon, a kaiser, or someone equally inspired. We

We all like the Minister of Railways, we like his style, and we feel that perhaps it is not so much the red-blooded Canadianism that is in him as his racial ancestry that makes him so fond of a fight. But on this occasion I am sure we are able to congratulate him upon the moderation of his views.
I should like very much to be able to say the same thing for his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I have a high admiration for the abilities of the Prime Minister, but I believe he does not always do himself justice in speaking in this house. He does not need to go to the extremes of ridicule and almost vituperation that he employs od occasions towards members on this side ot the house. Sometimes I think perhaps the Prime Minister does this with a purpose. I think he undertakes occasionally to give us a castigation in order that he may arouse the ire of members on this side and prolong the debate.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it may be asked why at this stage of the debate anyone should join in and prolong the discussion. Perhaps everything that can be said on the matter has been said. But I have no apology to make for taking part in this debate. I believe that, as has already been said, this is one of the most important problems that is before the people of Canada at this time. I do not admit that it is the most important problem; I join with some of the hon. members who have spoken previously in saying that the most important problem in Canada to-day is that of unemployment. But this question is to my mind next in importance, therefore I wish to put my views on record.
I desire to review shortly the provisions of the bill, explain in the briefest way possible my views with regard to them, and give reasons why I am going to appose the second reading. I feel I have a duty, as representative of a constituency the people of which are vitally interested in the railway transportation problem, to let my constituents know just where I stand and why I vote as I intend to vote. We have had many excellent speeches during the debate, and much valuable information has been put upon the records of the house. It it unnecessary to repeat information that has already been put on Hansard, so with the exception of a few figures which I will quote to bear out certain statements I shall make I do not intend to weary the house with figures.
The bill now before us affects not only the transportation system known as the Canadian National Railways, with which we as members of this house are more particularly concerned, and which is of such vital importance to large sections of our country, but also that other great railway system which we have in Canada, the Canadian Pacific. The Canadian Pacific is just as vital to the interests of Canada as the Canadian National, and in my opinion nothing should be done which will in any way interfere with the efficiency

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Totzke
of these two great roads. We have every reason to be proud of the great transportation systems of this country, greater than almost any others in the world. But the difference between our responsibility in connection with the one and the other of these two roads lies in the fact that representing the people of Canada we are directly responsible for the policies of the Canadian National, in spite of the statement of the Prime Minister a few days ago that the people of Canada really do not own this great railway. The service of these roads affects the economic life of the entire country. It affects eastern as well as western Canada, but to my mind it affects the western provinces more than it does the eastern provinces. The west is a country of great distances, rather sparsely settled. In eastern Canada the population is more concentrated, and the people have other means of transportation which they can use in case of emergency. In western Canada, if the weather is not propitious and our railways are not in operation, we are without transportation facilities. Settlement in western Canada in some instances followed the railways, while in other instances it went ahead of the railways, but where settlement went ahead to any great degree it was always with the understanding that eventually the railways would supply the transportation required. It is of vital importance to western Canada that adequate transportation facilities should be afforded, because of the very commodities we produoe. Every member of the house knows that our main products are wheat and other coarse grains, cattle and so on, and that it is necessary for us to ship those commodities over long distances. The only method of transportation available to us is the railways. It has been estimated that a farmer in western Canada who must haul his grain more than ten or twelve miles cannot do so at a profit. Of course at the present time, Mr. Speaker, if the farmer must haul his grain half a mile he cannot do so at a profit, but these are abnormal times and I for one am sufficiently optimistic to believe that conditions will improve.
I am entirely in favour of practising economy in the operation of our railways. Every business corporation and every business man throughout the world at this time is practising economy, and necessarily so. But we must be careful when we practise these economies not to go too far and jeopardize the very existence of this country. I am aware of certain duplications of service rendered by the two companies, and as I have already said I am ready to admit that in some cases
; Mr. Totzke.]
this duplication might be done away with, without impairing the efficiency of the service at all. I am afraid, however, that this mania for economy and for cooperation, for bringing together the two roads wherever there is the slightest suggestion of duplication, may be carried too far. It is my belief that at least a very large proportion of the people of Canada are opposed to any amalgamation of the two roads; I think the people want to see both roads prosper and give the service they were intended to give. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister state that there was no move towards amalgamation hidden in this bill, and the right hon. gentleman has promised to replace the section giving a definite assurance to that effect which was deleted in the Senate. I am afraid, however, that in spite of that clause the provisions of this bill are definitely leading towards the amalgamation of the two roads, but with that point I shall deal at greater length a little later in the course of my remarks.
A good deal of discussion has taken place during this debate as to where the responsibility lies for the condition in which our national road finds itself. A number of hon. members opposite have sought to put the blame upon the late administration, headed by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), but I think hon. members on this side of the house have succeeded in demonstrating that at least equal blame must be attached to hon. members opposite. But with this question of where the blame should be placed I am not concerned at all; the only thing with which I am concerned at this time is the possibility of getting our railways into a better financial position in order that they may give better service.
At this point in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay a tribute to the late Sir Henry Thornton. I am sure his death came as a shock to all members of the house. I went to Saskatchewan' about thirty years ago and have seen the railway development in that province since that time. Almost thirty years ago I moved to a town situated on the old main line of the Canadian Northern from Winnipeg to Edmonton, and I have lived there ever since. I was there during the time the road was being operated by the Canadian Northern; I was there when it was being operated by the Canadian National Railways before Sir Henry Thornton took charge, and I was there after Sir Henry became president. In all those years I have had a good deal to do with the movement of goods to and fro over that line, and I have had a good opportunity to study the service we were given. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that until Sir

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Totzke
Henry Thornton took over the management of the Canadian National railways we did not know what railway service was. Sir Henry Thornton was able to develop in the men working under him a spirit of loyalty and pride in the road which made all the difference between poor service and excellent service.
For a few moments now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with some of the provisions of the bill. As I said at the outset, I do not know that I shall have anything particularly new to contribute to the debate, but I should like to express my own views on some of these provisions and to make my position clear with regard to this legislation. Just here I might suggest that if the whips were withdrawn and hon. members opposite were allowed to vote according to the dictates of their conscience, and properly to represent the people of their constituencies, I am not so sure that this bill would pass this house. But if the bill passes part I will provide that a board of three trustees shall be appointed instead of the present board of directors. It has been said that this is the main portion, the most important part of the bill. With the view that a small board would perhaps function better than a large board I am inclined to agree, and whether it should be a board of three or five does not concern me very much. I rather agree with the suggestion that the smaller board could function better and with less delay than the larger one. I am not particularly in agreement with those who say that certain sections of the dominion should be given representation on that board, nor am I inclined to agree that any particular class should be represented, with the possible exception of labour, in view of the fact that it occupies so important a place in the working of the railways. But if we are going to appoint a small board such as this, the utmost care must be taken that only men of the highest integrity, men who have been zealous in public service and who have faith in the Canadian National Railways, should be appointed to the board.
Another thing I would emphasize is that if a board of three is to be appointed all three men should be full time officials. If we have only the chairman full time we shall find that the other two members of the board may not be sufficiently in touch with the affairs of the railway and may become more or less rubber stamps for him. Section 4 of the bill provides that the first board shall be appointed by the governor in council. To this a good deal of objection has been made; but here again I find that I have no particular objection to the government appointing the board of trustees
I believe that the government should appoint the board of trustees and I believe they should appoint their successors; in my opinion the government should take full responsibility for everything that is done by the board. Neither this nor any other government in Canada can pass the buck to anyone else. They must assume responsibility for the work of the board of trustees in carrying on the business of this great transportation organization. I too agree that there should be no political interference with the working of the board of trustees. But political interference and the assumption of responsibility are two different things, and again I say that we in this House of Commons are the elected representatives of the people who own this railway. It may be a technical point with the Prime Minister but it is not a technical point with me; the people of Canada own this railway, and so long as we pay the interest and keep up our obligations with respect to the system, the people continue to own it, and the government should take full responsibility for the appointment of the trustees and for their actions.
Section 7 of the bill deals with the removal of trustees. I find myself entirely opposed to this section. I think it is too cumbersome; it is too difficult to remove trustees in this way. Let me read the provision:
No trustees shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
It takes time to get the House of Commons together, and this is cumbersome and difficult as a means of rescinding an appointment of this kind; it is difficult to rescind such an appointment through action of the House of Commons and the Senate. Again I say that the government must accept the responsibility both of appointing and of removing trustees whenever there is cause for removal.
Subsection 6 of section 9 gives the trustees absolute power in all matters:
No order, regulation, by-law, act, decision or proceeding of the trustees shall require the approval of His Majesty or that of any other shareholder of any company to which this section applies.
Again I oppose this section. I regard this as a most unusual ancf dangerous power to give to any board of trustees. Sometimes similar powers are given to managing directors of incorporated companies, but they are always subject to review of shareholders at the annual meeting. This perpetuates the power of the trustees for at least the time of their appointment, or until they are removed from office, and according to the provisions of this bill

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Totzke
they may be reappointed to office and therefore be there in perpetuity. In my opinion therefore this clause is dangerous and most unusual, and once again I say that the government should take the responsibility. The cabinet acts as the executive for members of parliament. Members are here representing the shareholders of the railways, and to this clause I am therefore absolutely opposed.
Subsection 2 of section 11 is another provision with which I find myself in disagreement. It provides that the vote of the chairman must be included in a majority vote of the trustees. The majority vote of the trustees shall carry any resolution or any matter which may be under discussion, but in all cases where the trustees divide, the decision of the chairman shall be final. I could understand perhaps those who had to do with the drafting of the bill giving this power to the chairman of the board of trustees, if he were the only full time member of the board; but in that event there would be a one man board, a dictatorship for this great corporation, and he would have absolute authority to do whatever he wished. Should this bill receive the second reading, I suggest that this section should be amended in committee to provide that the decision of the majority of the board of trustees shall carry.
Section 12 provides that the budget of the Canadian National Railways shall be under the control of the trustees, and subsection 6 of section 9, as I have shown, gives them absolute authority to do whatever they may wish. Here again is an instance where the government should take responsibility and should have some control. Perhaps the late administration gave the railway company a little too free a hand; but we should profit by this experience and should therefore put a little more restraint on those who are now being appointed. But to say that to remove political interference means taking aw'ay the exercise of governmental authority is going too far. Subsection 2 of section 14 provides for the routing of freight through Canadian seaports:
The trustees shall so direct, provide and procure that all freight destined for export by sea which is consigned within Canada for carriage to national Railways either at point of origin or between that and the sea shall, unless it has been by its shippers specifically routed otherwise, be exported through Canadian seaports.
I am opposed to this section. I have nothing to say in opposition to the use of our Canadian seaports as much as and wherever possible, but I say that the board of trustees and the management of our Cana-

dian National Railways should not be handicapped in this way. They should be in a position to ship in a manner that seems the most feasible and most profitable at the time.
Part II of the bill deals with cooperation. The idea of cooperation is veiy good, and I do not think anyone will deny that economies can and should be practised. During this debate as well as during the past two years we have heard a good deal about the reckless extravagance of the Canadian National Railways. There has been extravagance by the management of that railway, but it was not the only railroad or institution in the country guilty of extravagance during the last two years. What about our friends the Canadian Pacific Railway? What about the Royal York hotel in Toronto and the Empress of Britain? I am sure hon. members will agree that there was extravagance in that company. If the prosperous times of 1929 had continued these things would not have been considered as extravagant.

Oh, oh.

do not believe this, all they have to do is to look at the trade figures and my statement

Why this legislation? This legislation is brought down in order to create a dictatorship in this country for the purpose of amalgamating the railways. I am prepared to take the interpretation of my hon. friend from Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), another bright legal mind from the province of Quebec, who says that he is in favour of the bill because he interprets it to mean amalgamation. The railways, from a revenue and business standpoint, I admit, are in an unfavourable position. But how about the farming industry? When I went home at the adjournment of the session last November I found that every farmer in western Canada who had produced a bushel of grain, raised a steer, fattened a hog or a turkey or a chicken, was disposing of all those commodities at a loss. But did that farmer tear up his farm in consequence? Did he tear up his fences? Did he quit farming? No, Mr. Speaker. When I went back home the land was all turned over ready for next spring. The farmers had gathered their hay into their barns to feed their stock during the whole winter, even though a grasshopper plague threatens to attack their farms in the spring. I say that the railways in this country, both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, have to do exactly as every other

No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
Suppose the House of Commons does pass an address asking for the dismissal of this trustee and the upper house refuses to concur; what then? Would the minister answer my question right now?

The upper house would not refuse if the trustee was breaking a law that had been passed by the parliament of Canada.
